item.title: 3 metro rail stations reopen after 2 hrs, road traffic returns to normal
item.description:
Readymade garment workers on Sunday blocked roads and staged protests in Mirpur, in the capital, demanding that the minimum monthly wage be raised to Tk 30,000.

They clashed with police repeatedly, with both sides chasing each other. At one point, protesters set fire to a police vehicle beneath the Mirpur 11 Metro Rail Station.

The clashes and chases took place between 11:00 am and 1:00 pm today. Police later dispersed the protesters by firing tear gas shells and sound grenades and charging them with batons, allowing traffic to return to normal.

Earlier in the day, around 8:00 am, workers from several garment factories blocked the road at the Mirpur 10 intersection, disrupting traffic in the area.

When police attempted to remove them, clashes broke out between the two sides at around 11:15 am. The two sides engaged in chases for half an hour.

According to witnesses, police repeatedly urged the workers to leave the road. At one point, the workers began throwing bricks and stones at police, who responded by charging them with batons and chasing them.

Police also used water cannons, sound grenades and tear gas shells to disperse the protesters.

The workers scattered but later regrouped and resumed throwing bricks and stones at police from different directions.

Around 12:30 pm, a police vehicle was set on fire beneath the Mirpur 11 Metro Rail Station. The fire damaged the metro rail station's water supply line. A gate on the eastern side of the station remains closed.

Khalid Hasan, a security guard at the metro rail station, said the Mirpur 10, Mirpur 11 and Pallabi stations were closed from noon to 2:30 pm following clashes between protesters and police.

Md Hanif, inspector (operations) at Pallabi police station, told Prothom Alo that the protesters left the road around 1:00 pm, allowing traffic to return to normal.

Earlier, Saiful Islam, a sub-inspector at Mirpur police station, told Prothom Alo that garment workers had gathered at several locations in Mirpur in the morning before blocking the road at the Mirpur 10 intersection.

Police were subsequently deployed to the scene, he added.

Garment workers had also blocked roads in Mirpur on Saturday, making the same demand. Traffic remained suspended from 10:30 am to 1:00 pm that day in Mirpur 10, Mirpur 11, Mirpur 12 and surrounding areas.

item.title: Banglalink transforms MyBL app into ‘Mukto’, opening services to all mobile users
item.description:
Banglalink is set to transform its MyBL self-service app into Mukto, a digital platform that will offer telecom services, entertainment and lifestyle features to users of all mobile operators, reports a press release.

The platform will allow users to sign in using social media accounts, local mobile numbers or international numbers, enabling access from anywhere in the world, according to a press release issued by Banglalink on Saturday.

Described by the company as Bangladesh’s first telco-agnostic digital platform, Mukto will bring together telecom services and a range of digital content, including music, stories, Islamic advice, news and sports.

The app will also feature artificial intelligence-powered personalisation to recommend products and services based on users’ interests and preferences. Users will be able to manage their own mobile numbers as well as those of family members and loved ones.

Kazi Mahboob Hassan, chief marketing officer of Banglalink, said the platform reflects the company’s focus on meeting customers’ needs beyond mobile connectivity.

“People do not organise their digital lives around telecom operators. They want technology that fits naturally into their everyday routines and makes life simpler, more convenient and more personal,” he said.

“With Mukto, we want to bring these experiences together in one place and make them accessible to everyone,” he added.

The initiative marks a shift in Banglalink’s digital strategy, from developing services primarily for its own subscribers to offering digital experiences to users across mobile networks.

The company aims to make digital services more accessible and relevant to everyday needs through the platform as it moves towards becoming a customer-first, digital-first technology company.

item.title: Bangladesh's foreign policy should be guided by national interests and aspirations of the people
item.description:
The Bangladesh Institute of Peace and Security Studies (BIPSS) hosted a fireside chat titled “Bangladesh’s Foreign Policy in a Changing World” in Dhaka on 31 October 2026.

The event featured Jahrat Adib Chowdhury, MP, chairman of the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Foreign Affairs and Member of the Executive Committee of the Inter-Parliamentary Union (IPU), as the guest speaker.

The discussion was moderated by Shafqat Munir, vice president and senior fellow of BIPSS. The event brought together ambassadors, diplomats, government officials, civil society representatives, and journalists.

In his opening remarks, Major General ANM Muniruzzaman, President of BIPSS, highlighted the rapid transformation of the global order, marked by growing multipolarity, geopolitical competition and the restructuring of global supply chains.

He noted that these developments present both strategic challenges and opportunities for Bangladesh, given its geographical position at the intersection of South and Southeast Asia and the growing geopolitical and economic significance of the Bay of Bengal.

He emphasised the importance of strategic autonomy and pragmatic multi-alignment, enabling Bangladesh to maintain constructive partnerships with different global powers while safeguarding its sovereignty and national interests. 

Highlighting climate diplomacy and humanitarian responsibilities, he stressed the need for continued advocacy for climate justice and sustained international engagement to secure a durable solution to the Rohingya crisis.

In her remarks, Jahrat Adib emphasised that Bangladesh's foreign policy should be guided by national interests and the aspirations of its people, rather than being shaped by competing demands from major powers.

She stressed the importance of making effective use of Bangladesh's relationships with global partners, including in trade, investment and economic cooperation, while maintaining flexibility in its international engagements.

She highlighted the importance of economic diplomacy, regional cooperation and stronger institutional capacity, particularly in the context of Bangladesh's LDC graduation. She also underscored the value of parliamentary diplomacy in building lasting relationships across countries and political parties, as well as  strengthening cooperation between parliament and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

The discussion further highlighted the need for pragmatic regional relations, stronger institutional support for migrant workers, and greater efforts to address irregular migration and protect the rights and welfare of Bangladeshi citizens abroad.

Participants further discussed the growing interconnection between foreign policy and national security. Issues such as energy security, border management, cybersecurity and regional stability require coordinated and forward-looking responses.

The discussion highlighted the importance of developing stronger institutional mechanisms and a comprehensive approach to national security.

In his remarks, Shafqat Munir emphasised the importance of maintaining Bangladesh's strategic autonomy by engaging with different partners and pursuing cooperation that best serves the country's national interests.

He also highlighted the need for a broader understanding of  Bangladesh's regional neighborhood, extending beyond its immediate land borders to encompass  wider South and Southeast Asian and maritime connections. He stressed the urgent need for a clear national security strategy and architecture, including the establishment of a National Security Council, to strengthen coordination between foreign policy and national security.

In his concluding remarks, he identified three key takeaways from the discussion: the growing interdependence between economic resilience and national security; the increasing importance of parliamentary diplomacy in advancing national interests abroad; and the need for strong institutions and accountability to support a credible and forward-looking foreign policy.

The event formed part of BIPSS's continuing efforts to facilitate dialogue on Bangladesh's evolving foreign policy priorities and contribute to informed discussions on the country's role in an increasingly fragmented and competitive global environment.

item.title: House of witness in crimes against humanity case attacked in Sunamganj, counter-allegations raised
item.description:
The house of a witness in a 1971 crimes against humanity case was attacked and vandalized in Shalla Upazila of Sunamganj, leaving five members of the family injured.

The incident took place at the house of Dulal Mia in Daulatpur village of the upazila on Thursday night. The family is preparing to lodge a formal case with the police station today, Sunday.

Dulal Mia is a prosecution witness in a case filed with the International Crimes Tribunal (ICT) in 2016 over allegations of crimes against humanity.

His father, Mamud Mia, was martyred during the 1971 Liberation War, while his sister, Jamila Khatun, has been officially recognized as a Birangana.

Dulal Mia alleged that after his shop was burgled, police arrived in the village to investigate upon receiving a complaint, which angered several local residents.

Furthermore, the accused in the war crimes case and their relatives had long harbored a grudge against him for testifying. He claimed that the attack, vandalism and looting were carried out out of that resentment.

However, the accused individuals and some local residents claimed that Dulal Mia's son and other family members were involved in the illicit drug trade and had previously served prison time in narcotics cases. They claimed that locals, frustrated by the ongoing drug trade, carried out the attack.

According to the victim's family, Dulal Mia's daughter, Ujala Akter and her husband, Helal Mia, live with him. The father-in-law and son-in-law jointly run a grocery shop in front of their house.

On 23 October, the shop was burgled. When the matter was reported to the police, law enforcement officers visited the spot to investigate on 29 October. After they left, several villagers expressed anger over why the police had been called to the village.

Dulal Mia alleged that around 9:00 pm on Thursday, a group of people, including Daulatpur village residents Jalal Mia, Abdul Hekim and their family members, attacked their house armed with sticks. The attackers assaulted family members, smashed household furniture, a television and a refrigerator, and looted six cows, gold ornaments and cash.

According to police sources, in 2016, freedom fighter Rajani Das of Perua village filed a case with the International Crimes Tribunal over charges of genocide, arson, rape and other crimes against humanity committed in Uzangaon, Shyamarchar, and Perua villages of Shalla upazila during the 1971 Liberation War.

11 people, including local figures Zubayer Munir, Zakir Hossain, Siddiqur Rahman, and Daulatpur village residents Abdul Hekim, Abdul Gani Mia and Tota Mia, were arrested in the case. Dulal Mia is a witness in this case.

Dulal Mia's daughter, Ujala Akter, told Prothom Alo over the phone on Sunday morning that the family members of Jalal Mia and Abdul Hekim carried out the attack and were still issuing threats. She said they were currently in Shalla Upazila Sadar and heading to the police station to lodge a case.

Accused Jalal Mia is the son of Abdul Gani Mia, an accused in the crimes against humanity case.

Denying the allegations, Jalal told Prothom Alo, "We are not involved in this. This family is known as drug dealers in the area. The local Anti-Drug Unity Council had repeatedly requested them to abandon this business, but they did not stop. That is why local people may have attacked them."

Police confirmed that allegations of narcotics trading exist against the family. Over the past four years, at least 25 cases involving drugs and theft have been lodged against them. Dulal Mia's son, daughter and son-in-law had landed in jail in narcotics cases.

Dulal Mia, however, asserted that his son, daughter and son-in-law were implicated in false cases and jailed solely because of his role as a witness in the war crimes trial. He claimed that the drug allegations are merely a smear campaign being used as a pretext for the attack.

Shalla Police Station Officer-in-Charge (OC) Mohammad Suhel told Prothom Alo at 12:00 pm on Sunday that the family is currently at the police station. He noted that police had advised them to file a case immediately after the incident.

"It is true that there are drug trade allegations against them, but that is for the police to handle. No one has the right to attack someone's house over that. Necessary legal action will certainly be taken once we receive a formal complaint," the OC said.

item.title: Garment workers’ protests: At least 80 factories shut in Gazipur and Savar
item.description:
Readymade garment workers staged protests in various areas of Savar and Gazipur, on the outskirts of Dhaka, on Sunday, pressing several demands, including an increase in the minimum wage to Tk 30,000. Amid the unrest, preliminary information indicates that at least 80 factories across the two districts have declared holidays.

The situation remained normal in the morning but began to deteriorate in Savar from midday. Police were deployed at various locations and outside factories to maintain law and order.

More than 50 factories in Savar declared holidays, said Mohammad Mominul Islam Bhuiyan, superintendent of police of Ashulia Industrial Police-1.

According to witnesses and officials of Ashulia Industrial Police-1, most factories were operating normally from the morning. However, workers at Al-Muslim Apparels in Nishchintapur, factories belonging to the New Age Group and Trouser Line Ltd stopped work and remained inside their workplaces.

At around 10.45 am, a group of workers from several factories took up positions on the Abdullahpur–Baipail road in front of a factory belonging to the Sharmin Group in Narsinghpur, Ashulia. They chanted various slogans demanding higher wages.

At one point, industrial police asked the workers to move off the road and stand to one side. The workers subsequently moved to the roadside and urged employees of the Sharmin Group to join them.

Amid the developing situation, the Sharmin Group factory management declared a holiday at around 11.45 am. Several other factories in the area, including those belonging to the Ha-Meem Group and New Age Group, also declared holidays.

Khairul Mamun, legal affairs secretary of the Bangladesh Garments and Sweaters Workers Trade Union Centre, told Prothom Alo that several workers, who had stopped working and remained inside their factories, had informed him that no representatives of the management had spoken to them about their demands.

As a result, the workers were unclear about the situation. He said workers at factories that declare holidays because of work stoppages often take to the streets in frustration when they are not given information about their demands. They also try to persuade workers from other factories to join them.

Mamun called for the situation to be taken seriously and urged the authorities to engage with the workers promptly.

At around 10:00 am, Ashulia Industrial Police-1 made an announcement over a loudspeaker mounted on a police vehicle.

The announcement said, “Industrial Police have always stood by you in this industrial area, providing peace, order and security services. Industrial Police are always working alongside our brothers and sisters among the workers to help them secure their legitimate demands and rights…”

Warehouse and pickup van set on fire in Gazipur

Amid the workers’ movement, a warehouse storing garment factory waste fabric and a pickup van were set on fire in Kaliakair, Gazipur. The incidents occurred in the Chandra Palli Bidyut area of the upazila between 11.30 am and 12.30 pm today. At least 30 garment factories in the area declared holidays because of the protests.

In the morning, workers from several factories, including Korni Knit Composite and Knit Asia in Ratanpur, Kaliakair, did not report for work and gathered on the highway near Shafipur Bazar. They began protesting after marking their attendance at their factories. Several nearby factories subsequently declared holidays because of the demonstrations.

According to witnesses, a pickup van was set on fire in the Palli Bidyut area at around 11.30 am. The vehicle was gutted as fire service personnel were unable to reach the scene because of the workers’ movement.

A short while later, a warehouse storing garment waste fabric belonging to a garment factory named Tropical was set on fire in the same area. After receiving the report, a unit of the Kaliakair Fire Service attempted to reach the scene, but the protesting workers obstructed them.

Mohammad Tariqul Islam, station officer of the Kaliakair Fire Service, said they had received a report that a warehouse belonging to the Tropical factory in the Chandra Palli Bidyut area had been set on fire. However, they were unable to reach the scene because of the workers’ protests.

Amjad Hossain, superintendent of Industrial Police in Gazipur, said efforts were under way to bring the situation under control. At least 30 factories in different areas had declared holidays.

item.title: In pictures: Police use tear gas, water cannons as garment workers clash in Mirpur
Difficult to keep Hasina silent due to India’s domestic politics
item.description:
C Christine Fair is a Professor in the Security Studies Programme within Georgetown University’s Edmund A Walsh School of Foreign Service. She previously served as a senior political scientist with the RAND Corporation, a political officer with the United Nations Assistance Mission to Afghanistan in Kabul, and a senior research associate at the United States Institute of Peace.  She has authored, co-authored and co-edited several books on security, societal changes and policing in South Asia. She recently addressed an international conference in Dhaka – the Bay of Bengal Conversations (BoBC) – where she was interviewed by with Prothom Alo Kolkata correspondent Suvojit Bagchi.

I spent some time in Afghanistan a while back. It seems almost impossible to resolve the ongoing conflict between Afghanistan and Pakistan. On the one hand, the Taliban claim territory up to Attock Pul on the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KPK)-Punjab border – a demand Pakistan finds entirely unacceptable. On the other hand, Pakistan accuses the Afghan Taliban government of sheltering the Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) cadres. Given this situation, what does the future hold?"

Christine Fair: It's an historical issue; when Pakistan became independent, Afghanistan took the opportunity to rubbish the Durand Line as an international border. The Afghan government argued that Pakistan is an illegal successor state, while the British said it is a legal successor state and the border is a legitimate one. But since (Pakistan’s) independence, every Afghan ruler has rejected the Durand Line. The Pakistanis were anxious to put some regime into place so that the Afghans would accept the Durand Line. That is why Pakistan kept supporting the Taliban. Pakistan hoped that the Taliban would finally accept the Durand Line as the border. So, that is where we are; while the Taliban have not accepted the Line, Pakistan continued to engage in hopes of settling the border. 

The Taliban leadership claims they are being targeted by Pakistani forces, but I got a sense that the TTP, the Afghan Taliban, and perhaps even Al Qaeda frequently overlap. How do you analyse this?

Christine Fair: Well, the Taliban is giving safe haven to the Pakistani Taliban and that is the core issue. This has been continuing. Even when Americans were in Afghanistan, they (Americans) could not expel Pakistani Taliban leadership from Afghanistan. The Afghan Taliban continues to create a safe haven for the Pakistani Taliban. That's why the Pakistanis are engaging in a military action against TTP redoubts in Afghanistan.

Isn't this support largely owing to the ethnic Pashtun connection?

Yes. They are generally Pashtun. But there is also a Deoband connection.

However, the Afghan Taliban also acknowledge that they found refuge in Pakistan for all those troubled years, leaving them somewhat indebted to Islamabad…

Christine Fair: Basically, the Taliban are trying to say that they are not giving them (TTP) safe haven, but that is not true. They also forced themselves on local communities in the tribal areas as you note, but essentially the leadership of the Pakistani Taliban is in Afghanistan. Like Lashkar-e-Taiba. The organisation operates in Kashmir but their high-level leadership is in Pakistan. 

Two parallel crises are snowballing in Pakistan: the Balochistan conflict and the widespread protests surrounding Imran Khan’s ongoing detention. Do these movements overlap, and what does the future hold for them?

Christine Fair: No. They are not overlapping. They are separate issues. 

The Baloch issue dates back to 1946 elections; there was no Baloch assembly (unlike in Sindh or Punjab). There were two kinds of Balochistan in 1946. One part was under British control with no provincial assembly. The Baloch got a provincial assembly as late as 1971 war or after the war.

The rest of Balochistan – initially under the Khan of Kalat – did not want to join Pakistan. Then he did so under duress and interestingly Jinnah was his lawyer, then (Khan of) Kalat changed his mind and Pakistan forcefully annexed Balochistan. Baloch never wanted to join Pakistan. We have seen Punjab, Sindh, East Pakistan – all went with Muslim League with the exception of Baloch who had no vote. Of course, the North West Frontier Province (now KPK) voted for Congress, essentially voting to stay within India.

Now, talking about the recent insurgency, it goes back to the time of President Musharraf. Musharraf actually was the one who brought Chinese development to Balochistan. There's this National Finance Commission of Pakistan that provides a pittance for Balochistan (for all these developments) because it is based on the population of the state; Balochistan got less because it's the least populated states but also one of the largest states geographically. They actually needed more development than was given by the Commission. So, there are no jobs and no opportunities. And whatever jobs and opportunities were there, it went to the Chinese. And Chinese are bringing in the workers, so this current crisis dates back to the time of Musharraf. 

Which way are the protests organised by Imran Khan’s party heading as the situation heats up?

Christine Fair: I don't think the Imran Khan’ issue is heating up. The army has a lot of discontent with the Imran Khan situation. The army has it under control and Imran Khan is not going to get out of jail, no matter what his supporters say. The only way Khan is going to get out of jail is if he agrees to go into exile, and so far, he has not agreed to opt for exile. 

So, are you saying the Pakistani government will be able to contain the situation despite these massive protests?

Christine Fair: It's not the government; it's the army and the intelligence services. They have been able to manage the situation. I am not saying I agree with it, but from my point of view, Field Marshal Asim Munir (army’s overall chief) has consolidated so much power that he is probably going to get away with it. That's my assessment. 

And is that because of the fact that he is immensely liked in Washington?

Christine Fair: Pakistan’s ability to control these crises has nothing to do with how much Donald Trump will accept or not accept (them). It is a whole separate issue. (Indeed) Washington enables him (Munir), but his ability to control the situation is independent of how much Trump likes him personally.

As seen during the BoBC, how deeply was the event focused on India-Bangladesh relations. Many private and public discussions were centered around former Bangladeshi Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, who is currently in India – Whether she can return to Bangladesh and what could be the possible impact. How do you analyse this situation, and what is the potential outcome of this impasse?

Christine Fair: I am a very practical person; I like to look at the facts on the ground. Ground facts as they are like this: yes, it is a political demand of the students and the BNP that India returns Hasina to Bangladesh.

That was the first question asked to the Indian High Commissioner (in BoBC), but the question is what will happen when she comes back to Bangladesh. The reality in Bangladesh suggests that executing a woman by hanging is quite difficult. And what she's going to do in jail? And then if she dies in jail, she becomes a 'martyr' to many. I would argue that the worst-case scenario for Bangladesh is if Sheikh Hasina returns to Bangladesh and dies here. It could create complications for the country’s politics.

From India’s point of view, India would love to see her leave India but no country will take her. And India is not going to hand her back over to Bangladesh under any circumstances.

Why so?

Christine Fair: Because she has proved to be a valuable asset to them all this while she was in power and there is no Extradition Treaty if the character involved is a political one.

In that case, there has to be a legal process to hand her over. For Bangladesh, it is better if she passes away in India rather than in Bangladesh.

Also, India has a long history of dealing with such situations, like dealing with the Dalai Lama or Aung San Suu Kyi (though she was not in formal exile). When India wants to keep a leader silent, it can.

So, the question is why do Indian authorities allow her to conduct provocative press conferences? That is the question I ask and the answer I get is not convincing; (they say) ‘well, we can't stop her, it is very difficult.’

Well, no, when you ask the Dalai Lama to stop making comments on China, he listens. Same with Aung San Suu Kyi. So why is silencing Hasina so difficult? This I think has a lot more to do with India’s domestic politics than international politics.

One last question. What do you think about the ongoing protests in India and what kind of impact it may have on the BJP led government?

Christine Fair: No comments on that.

Thank you.

Christine Fair: Thank you.

Five men took part in journalist Alif’s murder, Tajul fired the shot
item.description:
Two accused in the murder case of journalist Lutfuzzaman Alif in Durgapur, Netrokona, have given confessional statements before a court. They said Tajul Islam was the mastermind behind the murder and that five people directly took part in it. Tajul shot Alif with a pistol, they said. Police provided the information, citing the confessional statements.

The two accused, Imran Islam alias Imon, 24, and Sabbir Ahmed, 25, gave their confessional statements under Section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure to Nurul Amin Bhuiyan, senior judicial magistrate of the Durgapur court, on Sunday afternoon. The recording of their statements began at 3:45pm and continued until 7pm. The judge subsequently ordered that they be sent to jail.

Durgapur Police Station Officer-in-Charge Khandaker Shaker Ahmed told Prothom Alo that the two accused had said in their statements that Tajul Islam had a longstanding dispute with journalist Alif. The murder was committed as a result of that dispute. They used to work for Tajul as his associates and had various businesses in the border area. Alif obstructed their businesses and provided information to the police, which had also fuelled their resentment towards him.

The OC added that, according to the two accused, five people directly participated in the murder. Tajul Islam shot Alif with a pistol. After ensuring that Alif was dead, they fled the scene when people began arriving.

The OC said the statements also mentioned several people besides Tajul. Their names were not being disclosed at this stage in the interest of the investigation. Their identities were being kept confidential to facilitate the arrest of everyone involved in the murder, he added.

Police said at least 13 cases had been filed against Tajul over various offences, including murder, attempted murder, arms and drug offences, explosives, kidnapping, extortion, robbery and theft. His gang was also involved in smuggling along the border. He reportedly runs a criminal gang in the area under his own name.

Alif’s wife, Anandita Sangma, also known as Khadija Akter, previously told Prothom Alo that Alif had obtained information about Tajul’s arms and smuggling activities and passed it on to the Rapid Action Battalion (RAB). Around four years ago, RAB, now known as SRB, arrested Tajul.

In the last week of October, Durgapur Police Station OC Khandaker Shaker Ahmed told Prothom Alo that Alif had gathered information about Tajul’s various activities and published photographs and videos of his home on Facebook. Tajul believed Alif had also provided law enforcement agencies with information about the weapons he possessed. Alif had previously been attacked because of the resentment this caused, the OC said.

Journalist Lutfuzzaman Alif was shot dead on the night of 15 October in the Telonjia area near Utrail Bazar, along the Shyamganj-Birishiri road in Durgapur upazila. He was the Netrokona correspondent for private television channel Ruposhi Bangla. He also ran a Facebook page called “Detective Article”, where he published investigative reports on smuggling and other crimes and irregularities in the border area.

The day after the murder, Alif’s wife filed a case with Durgapur Police Station, accusing seven to eight unidentified people.

A team of the District Detective Branch (DB) police arrested Imran and Sabbir early Saturday from the Dhanpur Bazar area of Bishwambharpur upazila in Sunamganj. With their arrest, four people have now been detained in connection with Alif’s murder. Earlier, Sajibul Islam alias Apurbo was arrested on 18 October, and Ashikur Rahman alias Prangan on 20 October.

Netrokona Superintendent of Police Tarikul Islam told Prothom Alo, “The investigation has progressed considerably. We have established who else was involved in the murder. We hope to arrest them soon and bring them to justice. Details will be shared at a press conference afterwards.”

Alif’s wife starts job in Dhaka

Meanwhile, Alif’s wife, Anandita Sangma, also known as Khadija Akter, has joined a private hospital in Dhanmondi, Dhaka, as a nurse. Kayser Kamal, lawmaker for the Netrokona-1 (Kalmakanda-Durgapur) constituency and Deputy Speaker of Parliament, arranged the job for her. She joined on Thursday. Anandita has moved to Dhaka with her two children and mother.

Anandita, who belongs to the Garo community, was in a relationship with Alif. She converted to Islam when they married and later took the name Khadija Akter.

Speaking to Prothom Alo over the phone on Saturday night, Anandita Sangma said, “After the news was published in Prothom Alo, many people offered to help. A woman called me and offered assistance, asking for my bank account number. Since then, several others have called and assured me of their support. Now that I have a job, I do not need financial assistance from anyone else for the time being.”

Anandita added, “I want Tajul Islam, shooter Shamim and every other accused involved in this murder to be arrested quickly. They must receive exemplary punishment. I will never get my husband back, but I want to live to see the punishment of those who brutally shot him dead, orphaned my two children and left me without a husband. I want them to be hanged.”

item.title: Major (retd) Hafiz shown arrested in case involving 2 ex-army officers
item.description:
Retired Army Major Khandakar Abdul Hafiz, 56, has been shown arrested in a case filed against two former army officers—Debashish Kumar Barua and Kazi Gulshan Ara—on charges of involvement in anti-government activities, fund collection, and promoting violent digital content.

Detective Branch (DB) police arrested Abdul Hafiz from the capital's Banani area on Saturday night.

On Sunday afternoon, the investigating officer, Inspector Sheikh Bashir Ahmed of the DB Police’s Cyber and Special Crime (South) Division, produced Hafiz before the Dhaka Chief Metropolitan Magistrate (CMM) Court and applied for a seven-day remand.

Following a hearing, Dhaka Metropolitan Magistrate Rakibul Hasan granted a four-day remand.

According to the remand application filed by the police, the arrested Khandakar Abdul Hafiz, with the assistance of other accused individuals, was running anti-government propaganda on social media.

It further said that through a platform named 'Unity Care & Public Parliament' formed by several retired army officers, he was involved in state-subversive conspiracies and the rehabilitation of the Awami League by maintaining contact with former Army Chief General (retd) Aziz Ahmed, a former home minister, and absconding top leaders.

Furthermore, allegations were brought against him for inciting disorder from his personal Facebook page, spreading propaganda in favour of killing police officers, and communicating with domestic and foreign spies.

Police claimed that the accused had been systematically conspiring against the state since 5 August 2024.

Earlier, at midnight on 11 October, DB police arrested former army officers Lieutenant Colonel (retd) Bijoy Debashish Narayan Paul and Lieutenant (retd) Kazi Gulshan Ara from a residence in the Banani DOHS area.

The following day, Police Inspector Md. Ali Akbar of the DB’s Mirpur Zonal Team filed a case against them at Pallabi police station under various sections of the Cyber Protection Act and the Anti-Terrorism Act.

Bijoy Debashish and Gulshan Ara are currently in prison following the completion of their remand. Major (retd) Khandakar Abdul Hafiz has now been shown arrested under the same case.

At the time of filing, the case named Debashish and Gulshan Ara while listing 101 other unidentified individuals as accused. State Counsel Harun Or Rashid informed the court that Abdul Hafiz was shown arrested in this case after investigators established his involvement.

According to the case statement, the accused gathered at Kazi Gulshan Ara's residence at Pallabi to collect funds while associated with platforms named 'Bangladesh Awami League Supporters Alpha 1' and 'BBM Transparency'.

Additionally, they were using a Facebook page named 'KalAjkal.com' as well as personal accounts to incite violence and carry out defamatory anti-state propaganda, the case statement added.

item.title: Twin sisters emerge as the only GPA-5 scorers in entire upazila
item.description:
An unemployed father, financial hardship at home and the struggle to meet their education expenses could have stood in the way of their studies. But Rahima Sardar and Rabeya Sardar from Rajarhat upazila of Kurigram did not give up.

Through determination and hard work, these twin sisters scored GPA-5 in the 2026 Higher Secondary Certificate (HSC) examinations from the humanities group.

Their achievement stands out not only at their college, among the 14 educational institutions in the upazila as well.

Rahima and Rabeya are residents of Ramkarji village in Chinai union. They study at Rajarhat Government Mir Ismail Hossain College. The twin sisters had also scored GPA-5 in their Secondary School Certificate (SSC) examinations.

According to the college, 142 students from the institution passed the HSC examinations this year. Only two of them secured GPA-5—Rahima and Rabeya. No other students from the seven colleges, three school-and-colleges and four technical institutions in the upazila scored the top grade.

Their father, Monir Hossain Sardar, does not have a permanent job. He cultivates crops on a small amount of farmland and occasionally works as a seasonal day labourer. Their mother, Nasima Begum, is a homemaker.

The couple have three daughters. Their eldest daughter is married, while Rahima and Rabeya are the younger twin daughters. Despite the family’s financial hardships, the sisters continued their studies.

Their mother, Nasima Begum, said she was delighted with her daughters’ results.

“We have gone through a lot of hardship to educate our daughters. Private tutors taught the two sisters without charging any fees. The college principal took only nominal amounts for admission, form fill-up and various examinations. The girls also received stipends. Without everyone’s support, they might not have been able to achieve such good results,” she said.

Rahima Sardar, who scored GPA-5, said, “I studied with the aim of getting good results, partly to ease my father’s hardship and partly to fulfil our own dreams. Apart from the time spent travelling to college and eating, I spent most of the day studying. I also had limited time to sleep.”

Rabeya Sardar said their next goal was to pursue higher education at a good university.

“Now our dream is to get admitted to a good university and pursue higher education. We are preparing with that goal in mind,” she said.

College principal Professor Md Zahurul Islam said, “Among the 14 educational institutions in Rajarhat upazila, only these twin sisters from the humanities group secured GPA-5. We are delighted and proud of their achievement. On behalf of the college, I extend my heartfelt congratulations and best wishes to both of them.”

Sazzad Hossain, assistant upazila secondary education officer in Rajarhat, told Prothom Alo that four students in the upazila scored GPA-5 — two from the college stream and two under the Madrasah Education Board. The two students from the college stream are the twin sisters.

item.title: HSC results: Tamzeed scores 1,222 out of 1,300; study strategy he followed
item.description:
Tamzeed Tahseen appeared for the Higher Secondary Certificate (HSC) examinations in 2026 under the Chittagong board. According to the examination results, he scored 1,222 marks out of a total of 1,300.

Tamzeed passed the HSC examination from the science group of Chittagong University of Engineering and Technology (CUET) School and College. He is the son of Rezaul Karim and Shamsunnahar Begum.

Although his family is from Gaibandha, Tamzeed lives in the CUET campus area due to his father's profession.

Expressing his joy over the result, Tamzeed said, "It feels wonderful to secure the highest marks."

When asked if he followed any specific strategy while answering questions, he said, "I adopted a few tactics while writing my answers. I first answered the questions I knew best and tackled the relatively difficult ones later."

Regarding his exam preparation, Tamzeed noted, "There was no hard-and-fast rule about how many hours I had to study. I studied whichever subject I felt like reading at the time. Whenever I faced difficulty understanding something, I took help from my teachers. I approached them in person when needed and sometimes contacted them online. The teachers supported me wholeheartedly."

Noting that Chemistry is his favourite subject, Tamzeed said, "I enjoy solving problems in Physics and Chemistry. Driven by this interest, I want to study engineering in the future."

Tamzeed's father, Rezaul Karim, is a professor in the Department of Chemistry at CUET. Regarding his son’s performance, he said, "I have learned from various sources that he ranked first in the board based on total marks. Alhamdulillah. As a parent, this brings great joy. He put in the effort and he earned a good result accordingly."

Halima Khanam, acting principal of CUET School and College, told Prothom Alo, "We have learned that he secured the highest aggregate marks in the education board. We are thrilled with Tamzeed’s achievement. He is exceptionally talented and humble. He achieved this success through perseverance and diligence. This will inspire current students."

When asked about the claim of securing the first position, Chittagong Education Board Controller of Examinations Professor Parvez Sajjad Chowdhury said, "No merit-based rank list has been prepared, so it cannot be officially stated whose result was the highest. However, his result is undoubtedly commendable."

Students from Chattogram, Cox’s Bazar, Rangamati, Bandarban, and Khagrachhari districts sat for the HSC exams under the Chittagong board. This year, a total of 99,878 examinees appeared for the exams under the board, of whom 50,166 passed.

Female students outperformed male students in the pass rate, with girls securing a 53.49 per cent pass rate compared to 47.62 per cent for boys.

item.title: Where does all the money for political parties come from, Iftekharuzzaman asks
item.description:
A political party with a full organisational structure extending down to the union level across the country may need Tk 3.02 billion to Tk 3.93 billion annually to run its offices and activities. The estimated annual cost could rise to Tk 15.32 billion to Tk 21.88 billion if its organisation extends to the ward level.

However, there is a significant gap between these estimated operating costs and the income and expenditure figures disclosed by political parties.

The findings were revealed in a study by Transparency International Bangladesh (TIB).

The research report, titled “Institutional Governance of Political Parties in Bangladesh”, was released at a press conference at TIB’s office in Dhanmondi, Dhaka, on Sunday.

According to the study, the potential income from regular membership fees falls far short of the estimated cost of running political organisations. To bridge the gap, political parties rely on both formal and informal sources of funding.

At the local level, party activities are largely financed by local leaders and wealthy individuals. However, such expenditure is generally not reflected in the parties’ official financial statements.

Speaking at the press conference, TIB Executive Director Iftekharuzzaman said political parties require substantial funds to operate under the existing political culture.

Stating that the money is often managed through informal, largely individual-dependent arrangements, leaving considerable room for a lack of transparency, he said, "As a result, there is a significant gap between parties’ official financial statements and their actual expenditure."

Iftekharuzzaman also said abuse of power, black money and the criminalisation of politics were fuelling internal conflicts within influential political parties.

In many cases, political participation or party affiliation has turned into a “power-centred business model”, he added.

How much does it cost to run a political party

Based on information collected from leaders and activists of different political parties, TIB estimated the annual costs of maintaining party offices and conducting organisational activities. The study presented three estimates based on the extent of a party’s organisational network.

Under the first scenario, a party with the minimum organisational structure required for registration, including offices in 22 districts and 101 upazilas or police stations, would need Tk 140 million to Tk 250 million annually.

Of this amount, Tk 55 million to nearly Tk 70 million would be required to maintain offices, while Tk 85 million to Tk 180 million would be needed to organise political programmes.

Under the second scenario, a party with a full organisational structure extending across all 64 districts and 4,553 unions would require an estimated Tk 3.02 billion to Tk 3.93 billion annually.

This would include Tk 840 million to Tk 1.14 billion for office operations and Tk 2.18 billion to Tk 2.79 billion for organising programmes.

Under the third scenario, where the organisation extends down to the ward level within unions, the annual expenditure could reach Tk 15.32 billion to Tk 21.88 billion.

The estimates take into account the costs of maintaining offices at different levels, organising meetings and rallies, publicity campaigns, transportation and organisational coordination.

For office operations, the study considered regular expenses such as rent, electricity, water and hospitality. For political programmes, it assumed a minimum of five events a year.

TIB noted that actual costs could vary depending on whether party offices are owned or rented, as well as the nature, location and timing of political programmes.

How much can membership fees generate?

The declared sources of income for political parties include membership fees, donations and revenue from organisational activities. TIB also assessed whether parties could sustain their operations relying solely on membership fees.

Based on the membership numbers and fee rates specified in the constitutions of two political parties included in the study, a party meeting the minimum registration requirements could generate around Tk 2.6 million annually from membership fees.

However, the estimated annual expenditure for maintaining an organisation of that size ranges from Tk 140 million to Tk 250 million.

Similarly, a party with a full organisational structure extending to the union level could generate around Tk 375 million a year from membership fees.

For a party with an organisation extending down to the ward level within unions, the estimated annual income from membership fees could reach Tk 1.16 billion.

The findings suggest that membership fees alone are insufficient to finance political parties with extensive organisational networks.

TIB clarified that these figures represent estimated income and expenditure, not the actual financial accounts of any particular political party. Donations, nomination fees, special fundraising initiatives and other sources of income were not included in the membership-based revenue estimates.

Informal funding arrangements

The study found that political parties' fundraising and financial management largely depend on individuals.

Most parties collect money on an ad hoc basis to meet expenses related to meetings, conferences, political programmes, movements and elections.

At the local level, party offices, rallies, transportation for activists and other organisational activities are often financed by local leaders. Consequently, such expenditure is not reflected in the central financial accounts of the parties.

According to the study, businesspeople and wealthy individuals play a particularly important role in financing parties that are in power or have the prospect of coming to power.

In some cases, money is extorted from them. Others contribute substantial amounts in the expectation of securing party positions, electoral nominations or future benefits.

TIB said this financial dependence creates patronage-based relationships within political parties. As a result, economically influential individuals and groups gain opportunities to influence party decisions, candidate nominations and organisational activities.

Some political parties, meanwhile, collect funds at the grassroots through public donations or crowdfunding. Parties also generate income by selling nomination forms and publications, as well as from party-owned properties.

The study observed that substantial financial demands, coupled with the lack of transparent funding mechanisms, create risks of political corruption and the politicisation of crime.

Wide gap between declared income and actual costs

TIB highlighted a significant discrepancy between political parties' declared financial statements and their estimated organisational expenses.

The study analysed the 2025 financial statements of four political parties published in different media outlets.

Their declared annual income ranged from Tk 18.2 million to Tk 236.8 million, while reported expenditure ranged from around Tk 18.7 million to Tk 239.1 million.

According to TIB, these figures are extremely low compared with the actual costs of national-level political programmes, organisational operations and electoral activities.

However, the organisation noted that the declared financial statements of the four parties cannot be directly compared with the estimated operating costs calculated for different organisational structures.

The study also found that none of the political parties has a comprehensive and independent financial policy or financial procedures.

Parties do not regularly prepare annual budgets either. Although most party constitutions briefly mention sources of income and expenditure, they lack detailed provisions on fundraising, expenditure approval, fund management, internal controls and accountability.

Under existing laws, registered political parties must submit audited financial statements to the Election Commission every year.

However, TIB found that such audits often remain a formality. Actual financial transactions, sources of income and expenditure are not adequately reflected in audit reports.

The study also cited instances where newly formed or smaller political parties submit nominal or fabricated audit reports for fees ranging from Tk 20,000 to Tk 25,000.

The disclosure of financial information by political parties is also unsatisfactory.

None of the websites of the 16 active political parties reviewed in the study published annual financial statements or details of electoral expenditure.

Moreover, financial reports submitted by political parties to the Election Commission are not regularly made public, limiting people's access to information about the actual sources of party funding and how the money is spent.

TIB recommends reforms to ensure transparency

To ensure transparency and accountability in political financing, TIB recommended making the public disclosure of financial statements mandatory for all political parties.

It also called for all income and expenditure at both central and local levels to be included in party accounts, financial transactions above a specified threshold to be conducted through banks, and standardised accounting systems to be introduced.

The organisation further recommended empowering the Election Commission to scrutinise audited financial statements submitted by political parties and ensuring that audits are conducted by listed chartered accountancy firms.

Speaking at the press conference, Iftekharuzzaman said the July movement had raised expectations of an end to power-centred politics, but that change had yet to materialise.

Power-driven politics continues due to a lack of good governance within political parties, the use of money and muscle power, and a lack of accountability, he said.

He said political parties themselves must take responsibility for institutional reforms.

The TIB executive director stressed that party leaders must review their own activities to secure the future of democracy and regain public trust.

The research report was presented at the press conference by TIB Senior Research Fellow Md Julkarnayeen, Research Associates Kawsar Ahmed and Kazi Aminul Hasan.

Also present were TIB Adviser-Executive Management Professor Sumaiya Khair, Director of the Research and Policy Division Muhammad Badiuzzaman and Director of Outreach and Communication Mohammad Touhidul Islam.

item.title: Sabotage plot under guise of labour protest in Mirpur, 29 detained
item.description:
Police have arrested 29 people on allegations of setting fire to and vandalising a police vehicle during a road blockade by garment workers in Mirpur, Dhaka, demanding a minimum monthly wage of Tk 30,000.

They were arrested from different parts of Mirpur on Sunday afternoon.

Police alleged that Alif Mollah, nephew of former Mirpur lawmaker Elias Mollah, had mobilised more than 100 people and sent them to join the workers’ movement. They were allegedly involved in setting fire to and vandalising the police vehicle.

Of the 29 detainees, 11 were arrested by the Mirpur division of the Dhaka Metropolitan Police’s Detective Branch (DB). Police from different local police stations arrested the others.

A source in the DB police said local leaders and activists of the Awami League (whose activities have been banned in the country) were found to be involved in setting fire to and vandalising the police vehicle under the cover of the workers’ movement for their legitimate demands.

Mohammad Rakib Khan, deputy commissioner of the DB’s Mirpur division, told Prothom Alo that the detainees were followers of former lawmaker Elias Mollah and that some held party positions.

He said Alif Mollah had mobilised more than 100 people and sent them to the workers’ movement. They later acted together to set fire to and vandalise the police vehicle.

A DB source said the detainees had organised themselves through an online group and planned large-scale sabotage by using the workers’ movement.

Earlier on Sunday, garment workers blocked roads and staged demonstrations in Mirpur, demanding a minimum monthly wage of Tk 30,000.

Clashes and chases between the workers and police took place in several rounds from 11:00 am to 1:00 pm. At one point, protesters set fire to a police vehicle beneath the Mirpur-11 metro rail station.

Following the clashes, the Mirpur-10, Mirpur-11 and Pallabi metro rail stations were closed from 11:38 am to 1:58 pm.

9 arrested in Gazipur

Meanwhile, nine people have been arrested in Gazipur on allegations of instigating the workers’ movement. Police said they are leaders and activists of the Awami League and its associate organisations.

They were arrested during raids in different areas of Kaliakair upazila of Gazipur early on Sunday.

The arrestees are Yusuf Sikder, office secretary of the Awami League’s Kaliakair upazila unit; Sanwar Hossain, former general secretary of the Mouchak union unit of Jatiya Sramik League; Ariful Hossain, former vice-president of the Kaliakair upazila unit of banned Bangladesh Chhatra League; Masum Mia, organising secretary of Ward 9 unit of Bangladesh Krishak League and Mohammad Mehedi Hasan Mizan, an active member of Jubo League.

The others are Saiful Islam, Mohammad Russell, Shaikat Sheikh and Mizanur Rahman, whom police identified as active members of the Awami League.

Kaliakair police station Officer-in-Charge Shahidul Islam said the nine were not arrested simply for joining the workers’ protests. They were arrested following allegations of involvement in various acts of violence, he added.
